title: Math exercises for locomotion
html:
Mathematical equations

In this section we will use physics concepts and mathematical formulas for calculations

  • Linear velocity - the displacement of the body over time
    • Linear velocity = average of wheel speeds * wheel radius
    • Linear velocity = distance per revolution * rotational speed
    • Linear velocity = angular velocity * radius
    • Linear velocity = distance / time
  • Angular velocity - refers to how fast a rigid body rotates with respect to its center of rotation or axis.
    • Angular velocity = (right wheel speed - left wheel speed) / distance between wheels
    • Angular velocity = (π * diameter* rpm) / distance between wheels
    • Angular velocity = linear velocity / radius
    • Angular velocity = angle turned / time taken.
  • Revolutions per minute - measure of frequency of rotation. It states the number of full rotations per minute around a fixed axis
  • Maximum rotational speed - the maximum number of revolutions a rotating system makes within a defined period of time
  • Maximum linear velocity - the maximum rate of change of linear displacement with respect to time.

Other concepts and mathematical formulas

  • Degrees of freedom - defines the motion capabilities; number of joints or axes of motion on an object or robot
  • Cartesian degrees of freedom - the way objects are able to move along the three axes of a cartesian plane (X,Y, and Z)
  • Circumference = π * diameter
  • Distance traveled per rotation = Circumference
  • Degrees per distance = 360 degrees ÷ Distance traveled per rotation
  • Wheel rotation speed in radians = wheel rotation speed in RPM * 0.10472 rad/s
  • Distance covered = Linear velocity * Time
  • Number of rotations = distance covered / circumference

Math Problems

Question 1:

What are the Cartesian DoFs of a push lawnmower with four wheels? How is it still possible to mow an entire lawn with one, even though the wheels don’t yaw?

Question 2:

Is a car statically or dynamically stable? What about a motorcycle?

Question 3:

What are the Cartesian DoFs of an office chair with all caster-wheels?

Question 4:

What are the maximum Cartesian DoFs for orientable objects driving on the 2D plane?

Question 5:

What are the maximum Cartesian DoFs for objects that can freely translate and rotate in the world?

Question 6:

Calculate the Cartesian DoFs of a differential drive robot with two powered rear wheels and a central, front-mounted caster wheel. What happens when you add a second caster wheel?

Question 7:

Calculate the Cartesian DoFs of a standard car. How is it possible to still reach every point on the plane?

Question 8:

A steering wheel allows you to change the yaw of your car. Can you also change its pitch and its roll? See Figure 2.3 for reference.

Question 9:

You have a robot, a differential drive robot with standard wheels. The wheels have a diameter of 12cm and are 20 cm apart. Suppose that the left wheel of the robot is rotating at 13 rpm and the right wheel is rotating at 10 rpm per minute.

  1. Calculate the circumference of the wheels and find how many centimeters does the wheel travel per 360 degree rotation
  2. In order to travel 20 cm, how many degrees does the wheel need to turn?
  3. What is the linear velocity of the robot?
  4. What is the angular velocity of the robot?
  5. After 5 minutes, how much distance does the robot cover?
  6. What is the turn rate of the robot after 5 minutes?

Question 10:

Say you have a differential drive robot that has an axle length of 30 cm (distance between wheels) and a wheel diameter of 10 cm. Find the angular velocity for the left and right wheel if the robot is going to:

  1. Spin in place at a rate of 6 rpm
  2. Drive a circle of radius 1 meter (1 meter = 100 cm)
  3. Drive a straight line at 1 meter/min

Question 11:

Suppose you have a robot that goes at a linear velocity of 10.0213 cm/s. You know that the robots’ wheels rotate at the same speed and their radius is 4 cm.

  1. At what speed do the wheels rotate?
  2. How many rotations does the robots’ wheels need to take in order to travel 30 cm
  3. At what speed do the wheels need to rotate so that the robot is facing in the opposite direction in 5 mins?

Question 12:

A robot with an omni-directional drive system has four wheels arranged in a square. Each wheel has a diameter of 5 centimeters. Calculate the maximum linear velocity of the robot when all wheels are moving at their maximum rotational speed of 10 radians per second. Additional source: Omnidirectional wheeled robot example

Extra Question:

A differential drive robot has wheels that are 30 cm apart. Each wheel has a diameter of 10 cm. The right wheel starts rotating at 10 RPM and the left wheel at 15 RPM. After every minute, the right wheel increases its speed by 2 RPM and the left wheel decreases its speed by 1 RPM.

  1. What is the angular velocity of the robot in rad/s and the linear velocity of the robot in cm/s after 3 minutes?
  2. At what time will the robot start rotating in the opposite direction?
  3. If the robot continues this pattern indefinitely, what is the average angular velocity and linear velocity of the robot over the first 10 minutes?

Hint: The angular velocity can be calculated as the difference in wheel speeds divided by the distance between the wheels. The linear velocity can be calculated as the average of the wheel speeds times the wheel radius. Remember to convert RPM to rad/s when calculating angular velocity. 1 RPM = 0.10472 rad/s.
